content: Malabathrum, also referred to as Malobathrum or Malabar leaf, is the term historically used in classical and medieval literature to describe the leaves of the plant Cinnamomum tamala (sometimes identified as Cinnamomum tejpata). In ancient Greek and Roman times, these leaves were utilized to produce a fragrant oil known as Oleum Malabathri, which was highly valued. The leaves are specifically mentioned in the 1st-century Greek text Periplus Maris Erytraei as one of the significant exports from the Tamil kingdoms in southern India. In medieval writings, the term Malabathrum was also used to refer to the dried leaves of various trees within the Cinnamomum genus, which were believed to possess medicinal properties. In modern times, these leaves are commonly known as tejpat, tej pat, tejpatta, or tejpata in Hindi, and tamalpatra in Marathi. They are widely used in Indian cuisine, particularly in the Mughal-style cooking of North India. However, they are often mistakenly labeled as Indian bay leaves. It is important to note that true bay leaves come from the Bay Laurel tree (Laurus nobilis), a plant native to the Mediterranean region and belonging to a different genus. The physical characteristics and aromatic profiles of these two types of leaves are distinct. Bay leaves are shorter, light to medium green in color, and feature a single prominent vein running along the length of the leaf. In contrast, tejpat leaves are approximately twice as long, broader, olive green in color (sometimes with brownish spots), and have three prominent veins running along their length. True tejpat leaves impart a robust aroma reminiscent of cassia or cinnamon to dishes, whereas bay leaves have a fragrance more akin to pine and lemon. Indian grocery stores typically stock authentic tejpat leaves, but in regions where they are unavailable, some stores may only offer Turkish bay leaves as a substitute. Additionally, the bark of the Cinnamomum tamala tree is occasionally used in cooking, though it is considered inferior in quality compared to true cinnamon or cassia. The term Malabar refers to a region along the western coast of southern India, which corresponds to the northern part of the modern-day state of Kerala. The word Mala or Malaya translates to mountain in Tamil, Malayalam, and Sanskrit. The name Malabathrum is believed to have originated from the Sanskrit term tamālapattram (तमालपत्त्रम्), which literally means dark-tree leaves. Related Species: Cassia (Cinnamomum cassia) Cinnamon (Cinnamomum verum) Saigon cinnamon (Cinnamomum loureiroi)
